finding.headline: At 29, the 401(k) limit for 2027 is $25,500 and the IRA limit is $7,500.
details: The 401(k) limit rises to $25,500 for 2027, up from $24,500 for 2026. The IRA limit stays at $7,500.
You are 36 years from age 65, so you have many years to use these limits. Contributing up to the 401(k) limit each year is the main way to build savings in a tax-sheltered account.
Social Security benefits rise for each month you delay past full retirement age, but only up to age 70. Medicare sign-up is due at age 65, even if you keep working, to avoid possible extra cost.

finding.headline: About 20% of your pay goes to tax now; about 11% of withdrawals would in retirement.
details: Now, tax takes $12,142 of your $62,000 pay, so you keep $49,858. In retirement, the plan estimates $3,579 in tax a year on $30,324 withdrawn.
Draw on taxable savings and cash first, then your 401(k), and Roth accounts last. Your savings are 75% pre-tax and 25% taxable and cash, with no Roth yet.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Check the order with a tax professional before you withdraw.

finding.headline: You have no children, pets, or college costs to plan for, so your main costs are rent and debt.
details: Your basic yearly costs in retirement would be about $34,800, or $2,900 a month. Housing is the largest part at $21,000 a year.
Your student debt is $95,000. You pay about $3,000 a year on it, and about $6,412 a year in interest.
Your planned $20,000 roof in 2028 is the one big cost in your plan. Health costs before Medicare at age 65 are about $10,000 a year.

finding.headline: Plan for your money to last to age 96.
details: You are 29 and plan to retire at 65, so your savings must cover about 31 years of retirement. There is a 50% chance someone in the household reaches 90.
Your savings are small today, so steady saving and a plan for the $20,000 roof in 2028 matter most now.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Until you retire you save about $5,758 a year: $3,000 into a 401(k) or IRA, $1,500 from your employer's match, $1,258 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $25,000 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70, which pays about $31,000 a year.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 96. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
